statement: A strip is made of 4 equal squares in a row. How many rectangles of any size can be seen in the strip? A square counts as a rectangle.

choices.misconception: I counted only the four small squares.
I left out the four small squares because they are squares, even though squares count.
I counted the small squares and the two-square rectangles, then stopped.
I counted every size except the whole strip itself.

hints: Count the rectangles by how many squares long they are.
Every rectangle in the strip is a run of neighbouring squares. Count the runs that are 1, 2, 3 and 4 squares long separately, sliding along the strip each time.
There are 4 runs of length 1, 3 of length 2, 2 of length 3 and 1 of length 4.

solutions.reliable: Every rectangle in the strip is a block of neighbouring squares. Count by length: 4 blocks of 1 square, 3 blocks of 2 squares, 2 blocks of 3 squares and 1 block of 4 squares. That gives 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 rectangles. The transferable idea: count hidden shapes by size, and slide each size along the figure so that overlapping shapes are counted too.
solutions.elegant: A rectangle is fixed by choosing its left and right ends from the 5 vertical lines of the strip. There are 10 ways to choose 2 of 5 lines, so 10 rectangles.

whyOnTest: Hidden-shape questions test whether you count overlapping shapes of every size, not just the pieces the figure is cut into.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
